newsitem.title: ANGOLA: Angola smoulders in wake of Zaire revolt.
newsitem.headline: Angola smoulders in wake of Zaire revolt.

text.p: Foreign aid workers have pulled out of towns in eastern Angola threatened by fighting, which is linked to the recent civil war in neighbouring Zaire and may herald a government bid to knock out the rival UNITA movement.

Aid agencies in Luanda said on Tuesday they had pulled their people out because of mounting security problems, including an incident in which unidentified men detained an aircraft and threatened to set fire to it.

Fighting began three weeks ago with an offensive by government troops that could threaten Angola's fragile peace process. A 20-year civil war in the former Portuguese colony, one of the Cold War era's proxy conflicts, ended in 1994. But both sides remain armed and wary.

The government offensive coincided with the fall last month of Zaire's President Mobutu Sese Seko, who backed the UNITA rebels, and suggested that Luanda was seizing a chance to take back some UNITA territory, or possibly even destroy its rival.
The government says Angolan troops are simply mopping up armed units who fought on the losing side in Zaire's civil war and have since crossed its northern and eastern borders.
But analysts say this is clearly a pretext for moves to take control of diamond-rich areas long held by UNITA.
Aid agency officials said a U.N. World Food Programme (WFP) plane took six foreign relief workers from the towns of Luau and Cazomba in easternmost Moxico province on Sunday.
Their plane was held in Luau by about 20 angry men who stuffed grass into the aircraft and threatened to set it alight.
Both towns are controlled by UNITA. The aid workers pulled out after reports of troop movements at night along Angola's eastern border with the former Zaire, now the Democratic Republic of Congo.
The former rebel force still holds vast areas of the Angolan countryside, including the richest diamond areas in eastern Lunda Norte province, to the north of Moxico.

It was in Lunda Norte that the current offensive began, immediately following Laurent Kabila's victory against Mobutu, which had the active backing of the Angolan government. Relief workers say tensions then spilled over into Moxico and Malange.

They say more than half of a group of 4,500 UNITA troops have abandoned the Lunda Norte camp where they were disarmed last year under terms of the peace accord. They left citing concern for the safety of their families.

The United Nations, operating a peacekeeping force of 5,000 in Angola, was allowed into Lunda Norte by the government for the first time last Friday and reported seeing wounded in hospitals in three towns.

The government and UNITA joined a power-sharing government in April, but UNITA leader Jonas Savimbi, who reportedly sent some of his best troops in a vain bid to prop up Mobutu, has steadfastly refused to come to the capital where his longtime foe President Jose Eduardo Dos Santos holds sway.
Savimbi has been oddly reticent about the government raids into his turf, and Angola's national unity parliament was due to hold its first sitting on Tuesday, as scheduled.

Analysts say the former rebel movement is split between hardliners in the countryside who want to hold on to territory by force of arms if necessary and others open to political compromise and national reconciliation.
